title: The Movie Warner Bros. Tried to Bury Is Finally Yours to Watch
summary:
Picture this: you spend years making a movie, and then the studio decides to lock it in a vault forever. That's basically what happened to Coyote vs. Acme. Warner Bros. shelved the finished Looney Tunes film — reportedly as a tax write-off — until Ketchup Entertainment stepped in and released it in theaters. Now, starting September 29, 2026, you can rent or buy it at home on services like Fandango, Prime Video, and Apple.

The plot is exactly what the title promises. Wile E. Coyote files a lawsuit against Acme Corporation, the company that has supplied him with faulty gadgets for decades. Every rocket, every spring, every giant rubber band — they all blow up in his face when he tries to catch the Road Runner. So he takes Acme to court. Director Dave Green, who also helmed Earth to Echo and Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Out of the Shadows, blends live-action and animation, creating a world where cartoon characters are treated like marginalized citizens in human society. Think Who Framed Roger Rabbit meets a David vs. Goliath legal drama like Erin Brockovich or The Verdict.

The script comes from Samy Burch, partly inspired by a 1990 New Yorker article by Ian Frazier. Critics say it's zany, visually playful, and surprisingly touching. Wile E. Coyote, forever chasing and forever failing, becomes a metaphor for the indomitable human spirit. Even if the movie had been terrible, it still deserved to see the light of day. As the Road Runner would put it: "Beep beep!"

There's no word yet on a physical media release or streaming debut, but for now, you can catch it on digital. The film's anti-corporate message — that monopolistic corporations are not to be trusted and need to be actively kept in check — makes its shelving by Warner Bros. CEO David Zaslav all the more ironic. But thanks to Ketchup Entertainment, the movie is finally getting its moment.
why_it_matters: It shows how much power a handful of studios hold over what culture is allowed to exist: a finished film can be legally buried and only surfaces because a smaller buyer intervenes. For anyone growing up in a streaming economy, it raises real questions about ownership, copyright and who decides what audiences get to see.

background_read: Warner Bros. is one of Hollywood's oldest film studios, and it owns the Looney Tunes cartoons, a series launched in 1930 that gave the world Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck and the Road Runner. Wile E. Coyote and the Road Runner were created by animator Chuck Jones, whose shorts turned the coyote's endless failures into comedy.

Studios sometimes cancel completed films for financial reasons: writing a movie off as a tax loss can be worth more than releasing a weak performer. Coyote vs. Acme was finished and then shelved, and the decision drew unusually loud criticism from filmmakers and fans who saw it as a finished work being buried.

The film's courtroom plot echoes earlier mixes of animation and live action. Who Framed Roger Rabbit (1988) placed cartoon characters in a human world, while legal dramas such as Erin Brockovich build their stories around ordinary people taking on giant companies.

Warner Bros. Discovery CEO David Zaslav (the executive in charge of the company) became a symbol of aggressive cost-cutting, and Ketchup Entertainment (a smaller independent distributor) later picked the movie up — a reminder that independent companies sometimes rescue projects the big studios give up on.

perspectives.description: They see the release as a win for audiences and for the people who made the movie. Public pressure, plus a distributor willing to take a risk, rescued years of work that a corporation had written off as an accounting entry.

They argue the episode exposes how casually studios treat art as a line item. If a tax write-off is worth more than a release, the incentive is to bury films quietly, and the creators and crews are the ones who lose.

Shelving finished projects is not new — Warner Bros. also scrapped its completed Batgirl film rather than release it, and studios have cancelled films for decades. What is changing is that fans now hear about it instantly and can organise pushback.

The next questions are practical: will the film get a physical media or streaming release, and will the tax-write-off loophole be tightened or simply become standard practice? The answer will shape whether more buried films ever resurface.
